title: Build a 3-Tier WordPress Website on AWS (VPC, ALB, EC2, RDS, EFS)
summary:
Running WordPress on one server is easy. Running it in a way that is secure, redundant and ready to scale is where the learning happens. In this tutorial we build a traditional 3-tier architecture on AWS by hand, using the console, so you understand what every service does.

This project is based on the "Traditional 3-Tier WordPress website Deployment on AWS" project from Tech With Lucy's 5 Advanced AWS Cloud Projects course. I added fixes and extra notes along the way.

What we are building

Tier Components Location
Entry Application Load Balancer, NAT Gateways 2 public subnets
Application 2 EC2 instances (Apache, PHP, WordPress) 2 private subnets
Data Amazon RDS for MySQL, Amazon EFS 2 private subnets

A visitor reaches the Application Load Balancer through the Internet Gateway. The ALB forwards requests to two private EC2 instances in different Availability Zones. WordPress stores its data in RDS and its files (themes, plugins, uploads) on a shared EFS volume, so both servers always serve the same content.

Prerequisites
An AWS account and the us-east-1 region selected
An EC2 key pair (.ppk for PuTTY or .pem for a normal SSH client)
Basic comfort with the AWS console and a terminal

Part A: Networking

Step 1: Create the VPC


Open the VPC console and choose Create VPC → VPC only.
Name tag: MyVPC
IPv4 CIDR: 10.0.0.0/16, tenancy: Default.
After creating it, choose Actions → Edit VPC settings and enable DNS hostnames.

Step 2: Create and attach the Internet Gateway

Go to Internet Gateways → Create internet gateway and name it MyIGW.
Select it, choose Actions → Attach to VPC, and pick MyVPC.

Step 3: Create six subnets


Create these in MyVPC (Subnets → Create subnet):

Name AZ CIDR
PublicSubnet1 us-east-1a 10.0.0.0/24
PublicSubnet2 us-east-1b 10.0.1.0/24
PrivateAppSubnet1 us-east-1a 10.0.2.0/24
PrivateAppSubnet2 us-east-1b 10.0.3.0/24
PrivateDBSubnet1 us-east-1a 10.0.4.0/24
PrivateDBSubnet2 us-east-1b 10.0.5.0/24

Step 4: Create route tables


PublicRouteTable: add the route 0.0.0.0/0 → MyIGW, then associate PublicSubnet1 and PublicSubnet2.
PrivateRouteTableAZ1: associate PrivateAppSubnet1 and PrivateDBSubnet1.
PrivateRouteTableAZ2: associate PrivateAppSubnet2 and PrivateDBSubnet2.

Step 5: Create the NAT Gateways


Private instances need outbound internet access for package installs, but nothing should be able to start a connection to them.

Go to Elastic IPs and allocate two addresses.
Create NATGateway1 in PublicSubnet1 with the first Elastic IP.
Create NATGateway2 in PublicSubnet2 with the second Elastic IP.
Add 0.0.0.0/0 → NATGateway1 to PrivateRouteTableAZ1, and 0.0.0.0/0 → NATGateway2 to PrivateRouteTableAZ2.
Step 6: Create the security groups


Create all five in MyVPC. Each group trusts the group in front of it instead of an IP range.

Name Inbound rules
ALBSecurityGroup HTTP 80 and HTTPS 443 from 0.0.0.0/0
WebServerSecurityGroup HTTP 80 and HTTPS 443 from ALBSecurityGroup
DatabaseSecurityGroup MySQL 3306 from WebServerSecurityGroup
EFSSecurityGroup NFS 2049 from WebServerSecurityGroup, plus NFS 2049 from EFSSecurityGroup itself (self-referencing)
SSHSecurityGroup SSH 22 from My IP

Leave outbound rules as "allow all".

Part B: Database and shared storage

Step 7: Create the DB subnet group and RDS instance


In RDS → Subnet groups, create MyDBSubnetGroup with MyVPC and the two DB subnets (10.0.4.0/24, 10.0.5.0/24).
Choose Create database → Standard create → MySQL (8.0.x) → Free tier.
DB instance identifier: MyMySQLDatabase. Master username: admin, with a strong password.
Connectivity: MyVPC, subnet group MyDBSubnetGroup, Public access: No, security group DatabaseSecurityGroup.
Additional configuration: initial database name mydatabase.
When it is available, copy the endpoint. You will need it for DB_HOST.

Step 8: Create the EFS file system


Open EFS → Create file system, name it MyEFS, select MyVPC, and choose Customize.
Create mount targets in PrivateAppSubnet1 and PrivateAppSubnet2 and attach EFSSecurityGroup.
Copy the file system DNS name (it looks like fs-xxxx.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com).

Part C: Setup server and WordPress

Step 9: Launch a temporary setup instance


This instance in a public subnet lets us install WordPress once onto EFS.

Name: Webserver-Instance, Amazon Linux, t2.micro
Key pair: your key pair
Network: MyVPC, PublicSubnet1, auto-assign public IP enabled
Security groups: SSHSecurityGroup and WebServerSecurityGroup

Step 10: Connect over


With PuTTY, load your .ppk under Connection → SSH → Auth → Credentials and connect to ec2-user@. With a terminal:

bash
ssh -i MyKeyPair.pem ec2-user@

Step 11: Mount EFS and install WordPress


Replace with your file system DNS name.

bash
sudo su
yum update -y
yum install -y nfs-utils httpd php php-mysqlnd php-gd php-xml php-mbstring php-intl php-zip php-curl
mkdir -p /var/www/html
mount -t nfs4 -o nfsvers=4.1,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,hard,timeo=600,retrans=2,noresvport :/ /var/www/html
systemctl enable --now httpd

wget https://wordpress.org/latest.tar.gz
tar -xzf latest.tar.gz
cp -r wordpress/* /var/www/html/
cp /var/www/html/wp-config-sample.php /var/www/html/wp-config.php
nano /var/www/html/wp-config.php

In wp-config.php set:

php
define( 'DB_NAME', 'mydatabase' );
define( 'DB_USER', 'admin' );
define( 'DB_PASSWORD', 'your-password' );
define( 'DB_HOST', 'your-rds-endpoint' );

Save (Ctrl+X, Y, Enter), then:

bash
chown -R apache:apache /var/www/html
systemctl restart httpd

Open http:// in a browser and finish the WordPress installer (site title, admin user, password, email).

Part D: App servers and load balancer

Step 12: Launch two private app servers


Launch ApplicationServer1 in PrivateAppSubnet1 and ApplicationServer2 in PrivateAppSubnet2:

t2.micro, same key pair
Security group: WebServerSecurityGroup
No public IP

Paste this into Advanced details → User data for both (replace ):

bash

!/bin/bash

yum update -y
yum install -y nfs-utils httpd php php-mysqlnd php-gd php-xml php-mbstring php-intl php-zip php-curl
mkdir -p /var/www/html
echo ":/ /var/www/html nfs4 nfsvers=4.1,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,hard,timeo=600,retrans=2,_netdev 0 0" >> /etc/fstab
mount -a
systemctl enable --now httpd
systemctl restart httpd

Both servers mount the same EFS volume, so they already have WordPress and the same configuration.

Note: the original course script also installs a MySQL server. It is not needed because the database runs on RDS.

Step 13: Create the target group and load balancer


EC2 → Target Groups → Create: type Instances, name MyAppServers, HTTP 80, MyVPC. Register both app servers.
EC2 → Load Balancers → Create → Application Load Balancer:
Name MyALB, Internet-facing
VPC MyVPC, subnets PublicSubnet1 and PublicSubnet2
Security group ALBSecurityGroup
Listener HTTP 80 forwarding to MyAppServers

Step 14: Test and finish


Wait until both targets show healthy, then open the ALB's DNS name in your browser.
Log in at http:///wp-admin.
Go to Settings → General and set both WordPress Address and Site Address to http://.
Terminate Webserver-Instance. It is no longer needed.

You now have a WordPress site where the only public component is the load balancer, the app servers have no public IPs, and the database is reachable only from the web tier.

Troubleshooting

Targets unhealthy: check that Apache is running, EFS mounted, and WebServerSecurityGroup allows port 80 from ALBSecurityGroup.
EFS mount times out: check port 2049 in EFSSecurityGroup.
"Error establishing a database connection": check DB_HOST and that DatabaseSecurityGroup allows 3306 from the web servers.
Packages fail to install on private servers: the NAT Gateway routes are missing or wrong.

Conclusion

Building this by hand teaches the ideas behind most AWS web architectures: network isolation, least-privilege traffic rules, shared storage, a managed database and a load balancer in front. If this helped, drop a comment with what you would add, and let me know where you got stuck.

title: Black Friday 2026: how to spot a fake online shop in 60 seconds, before you pay
summary:
The dates: Black Friday is on Friday, 27 November 2026, Cyber Monday on 30 November. Many retailers start their discounts on Monday, 23 November. These are the days when lots of new shops appear with brand-name goods at dream prices, and then comes the second wave: fake delivery texts and “your order” emails.

The 60-second check before you buy

  1. Price: a brand product for half of what everyone else charges, or less? Check a price comparison site. If the price is only that low in this one shop, it is not a bargain, it is a warning sign.
  2. Read the address carefully: does it contain a brand name with extras like -outlet, -sale or a country name, or an ending such as .shop or .top? Real brands almost always sell under their well-known address.
  3. Company details: full company name, a real street address, a company registration or VAT number. Look the address up on a map: a private house, a mailbox service or a completely different business is a bad sign.
  4. Payment options at checkout: the home page often shows PayPal, cards and invoice. What matters is what is really left at checkout. Only bank transfer in advance, crypto or gift cards: stop.
  5. Click the trust badge: a real badge opens a certificate on the badge issuer's own site, naming exactly this shop. A badge that is only a picture is worthless.
  6. Reviews outside the shop: search for the shop name plus “reviews” or “scam”. Five stars on its own page and nothing anywhere else: be careful.
  7. Consumer services: many countries have a free checker or warning list run by a consumer organisation, for example the Fakeshop-Finder of the German Verbraucherzentrale. It does not know every new shop, but it knows many.

No single point proves anything. Two or three warning signs together are enough for me not to order.

The padlock in the browser proves nothing

The padlock only means the connection is encrypted. Anyone can get a certificate for free in a few minutes, scammers included. With the SSL certificate checker you can at least see since when the certificate is valid and for which names. A certificate that is a few days old, on a shop that claims to have been selling “since 2009”, does not add up.

For the tech-curious: two checks hardly anyone does

  • The domain's mail setup: a real shop sends order confirmations and usually has SPF and DMARC set up for that. The mail DNS checker shows this in seconds. If everything is missing, that is not proof, but it is one more warning sign.
  • Security headers: big shops usually send a few protective headers. The security headers checker shows what a site sends. How well-known German shops score is in the header ranking.

After the purchase: the second wave

If you order during Black Week, you are waiting for parcels. The next scams build on exactly that:

  • Delivery texts saying “delivery failed, please pay a small fee”.
  • Amazon and PayPal phishing emails about an order you never placed.
  • When you sell on classified ads: the fake buyer with a “safe payment” link.

The rule stays simple: do not tap the link in the message. Open the app or the retailer's site yourself and check there. If you are unsure, paste the message into my scam check. The scam radar shows which scams are running right now, updated twice a day.

Already paid? Act now

  1. Call your bank, right away. For a bank transfer it can try a recall, which only works while the money has not been withdrawn yet.
  2. Card payment: ask your bank for a chargeback. Direct debits in the SEPA area can be returned within eight weeks without a reason.
  3. PayPal: open a buyer protection case. Note: payments “to friends and family” are not covered.
  4. Keep evidence: screenshots of the shop, the order, the emails and the payment.
  5. Report it to the police; in many countries this works online.
  6. If you entered a password there that you also use elsewhere: change it everywhere. The password generator makes a safe replacement.

The full list of warning signs is in my guide how to spot a fake online shop.

The short version to pass on

Too cheap, odd address, no real company details, only payment in advance at checkout: do not buy. Do not tap links in delivery texts and order emails, check in the app yourself. And if it has already happened: call the bank at once. Feel free to send this to parents and friends who shop online this week.

Originally published at daniele-michelin.com. More guides, free checks (SPF, TLS, headers) and an error-message lexicon: daniele-michelin.com/en/.

title: GitHub Actions "Canceling since a higher priority waiting request exists": Concurrency Settings for CI vs Deploys
summary:
Short answer: that message means a concurrency group is working as designed. GitHub allows one running and one pending run per group, and a newer pending run replaces the older pending one. For CI you usually want that. For deploys you usually don't, so set cancel-in-progress: false on deploy workflows and key the group to the thing you're protecting (an environment), not to the branch.

What does the message actually mean?

You push twice in quick succession, and the first run's annotation reads:

Canceling since a higher priority waiting request for 'CI-refs/heads/main' exists

or the run is simply marked "Canceled" with no step failing. Nothing is broken. A workflow like this caused it:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

The rules, as documented by GitHub as of late 2026:

  • Per concurrency group, at most one run is in progress and at most one is pending.
  • If a new run arrives while one is already pending, the older pending run is canceled. This happens even when cancel-in-progress is false.
  • With cancel-in-progress: true, the new run also cancels the one that's currently running.

That second bullet is what surprises people. Without cancel-in-progress, runs queue, but the queue is one deep. Push three commits fast and the middle one disappears.

Takeaway: a concurrency group is a one-slot queue, not an unbounded one, so anything you can't afford to skip must not share a group with newer work.

Why did my deploy get canceled halfway?

The common failure: someone copies the CI snippet above into a deploy workflow. Commit A starts deploying (migration running, half the containers swapped). Commit B lands, cancel-in-progress: true kills A mid-step, and B starts against a half-migrated environment. The cancellation is clean from GitHub's point of view, but your infrastructure isn't transactional.

Typical dead ends:

  1. Adding if: always() cleanup steps. Cancellation does run always() steps, but you can't undo a half-applied migration from a cleanup step.
  2. Removing concurrency entirely. Now two deploys can run at once and race each other, which is worse.
  3. Using github.sha in the group name. Every commit gets its own group, so nothing serializes. It looks like concurrency control but does nothing.

The fix is to serialize without canceling:

name: deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh

Now deploy A finishes, then the newest pending commit deploys. If three commits arrive during A, the middle one is dropped, which is fine here because the last one contains it. Deploys of every commit in order would need a different design (a real queue), but "deploy the latest main" is what most teams want.

Takeaway: for deploys, key the group to the target environment and turn cancellation off; let the one-slot queue skip stale commits instead of killing in-flight ones.

How should I configure CI and deploy differently?

Workflow Group key cancel-in-progress Why
PR tests/lint workflow + PR ref true Old commit's results are obsolete
Push to main (tests) workflow + ref false You want a result for each main commit, at least the latest
Deploy fixed per environment false Never kill a deploy mid-flight
Scheduled/cron jobs fixed per job false Overlap risk, but skipping a run beats killing one
Docs/preview builds workflow + PR ref true Only the latest preview matters

The pattern I use for a single CI file that handles both PRs and main, so you cancel on PRs but never on main:

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

The || fallback matters. On push events github.event.pull_request.number is empty, so the group falls back to the ref. On pull requests, using the PR number is more stable than github.ref (refs/pull/N/merge) and groups runs the same way if you later add other triggers.

Takeaway: one expression, cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}, gives you cancel-on-PR and never-cancel-on-main from a single block.

What are the gotchas with concurrency groups?

  • Group names are shared across the whole repository, not per workflow. Two workflows that both say group: production will block each other. That's useful when intentional (a deploy and a rollback workflow sharing a lock) and a confusing stall when accidental. Include github.workflow in the name unless you want sharing.
  • Job-level concurrency exists too. You can put concurrency on a single job, e.g. only the deploy job, while tests in the same workflow run freely. A pending job waits with status "Queued" and no logs, which looks like a hang.
  • Required checks and canceled runs. A canceled run doesn't satisfy a required status check, but the newer run for the same PR will. The trap is canceling on main when branch protection or a downstream workflow depends on every commit's result.
  • Group names are case-insensitive per GitHub's docs, so Deploy and deploy collide.
  • Self-hosted runner queues are separate. Concurrency is about workflow runs, not runner capacity; a run can be "not canceled" and still wait for a runner.

I'd verify behavior once on a throwaway branch: push two commits within seconds with a sleep 60 step, and watch which run survives. It takes five minutes and removes the guesswork.

Takeaway: concurrency groups are repo-wide names, so a typo'd or duplicated group is a lock shared with workflows you forgot about.

FAQ

Why does GitHub Actions cancel my workflow run even though I didn't cancel it?
A concurrency block with cancel-in-progress: true cancels the running job when a newer run enters the same group. Even without it, a newer pending run replaces an older pending one.

Does cancel-in-progress: false queue every run?
No. Only one run can be pending per group, so extra runs in a burst are canceled in favor of the newest. Use a separate queue mechanism if every commit must deploy in order.

What should the concurrency group be for a deploy workflow?
A fixed string per target environment, such as deploy-production, with cancel-in-progress: false. Don't include the commit SHA or branch, or nothing will be serialized.

Bottom line

Use cancel-in-progress for anything whose result becomes obsolete when a newer commit arrives: PR tests, lint, preview builds. Use a fixed per-environment group with cancellation off for deploys, migrations, and anything that mutates real infrastructure. If you need every commit deployed in order, a concurrency group isn't enough and you need an actual queue.

title: 3-Tire WordPress website Deployment on AWS
summary:
Deploying WordPress on AWS with a 3-Tier Architecture

Hosting WordPress on one server works until that server crashes, traffic spikes, or the database is exposed to the internet. This article walks through how I built WordPress the way real companies do: a secure, scalable 3-tier architecture on AWS, step by step and in plain language.

The project is split into six parts, which this article follows in order:

  1. Project Overview
  2. Networking Setup: create a V
  3. Networking Setup: create a NAT Gateway and security groups
  4. Database Setup: create a MySQL database and EFS in AWS
  5. Compute Setup: set up EC2 instances and an Application Load Balancer
  6. Conclusion and Clean-up What is a 3-tier architecture? A 3-tier architecture splits an application into three layers, and each layer has one job. Think of a restaurant: customers meet the host at the door, the kitchen prepares the food, and the storage room keeps the ingredients. Customers never walk into the kitchen or the storage room. Tier Restaurant analogy In this project Presentation The front door and host Application Load Balancer in public subnets Application The kitchen Two EC2 instances running WordPress in private subnets Data The storage room Amazon RDS (MySQL) in private subnets This separation is what makes the design secure and reliable. Only the Load Balancer faces the internet, so the servers and the database cannot be reached directly from outside. Part 1: Project Overview The goal is a live WordPress website that stays available if one server or one data centre fails, and that keeps its servers and database hidden from the public internet. The build has five main pieces: • Network setup: a VPC with 2 public and 4 private subnets. An Internet Gateway gives the public subnets internet access, and 2 NAT Gateways in the public subnets give private resources outbound-only access. • Load balancing: an Application Load Balancer (ALB) receives visitor traffic and spreads it across the servers. • Compute layer: two EC2 instances in private subnets host the WordPress application. • Database layer: an Amazon RDS MySQL instance in the private subnets stores the site data. • Routing and security: route tables and security groups control which traffic may flow where. Visitors enter through the Internet Gateway and reach the Load Balancer, which forwards requests to the WordPress servers. The servers use EFS for files and RDS for data, and the NAT Gateways give the private subnets outbound-only access. Services used Service What it does here Category Amazon VPC Isolated network with subnets, route tables and NAT Gateways Networking Internet Gateway Gives public subnets access to the internet Networking NAT Gateway Lets private instances download updates without being exposed Networking Application Load Balancer Distributes incoming traffic across the EC2 instances Load balancing Amazon EC2 Runs the WordPress application Compute Amazon RDS Managed MySQL database for WordPress data Database Amazon EFS Shared file storage so both servers see the same WordPress files Storage IAM roles and policies Secure permissions between AWS services Permissions Route tables Direct traffic between subnets, gateways and the internet Networking Security groups Fine-grained firewall rules for each resource Security What the finished project delivers • A live WordPress website reachable through the ALB DNS name • Secure traffic routing, with EC2 instances kept in private subnets • An integrated Amazon RDS database for dynamic content • A scalable, production-style 3-tier architecture Part 2: Networking Setup, VPC with Public and Private Subnets The VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is your own isolated network inside AWS, and every other resource in this project lives inside it. I split it into 2 public and 4 private subnets, spread across two Availability Zones so that an outage in one zone does not take the site down. The CIDR ranges below are an example layout. Use any non-overlapping ranges you prefer. Subnet Type Availability Zone Purpose Example CIDR public-1 Public AZ 1 Load Balancer, NAT Gateway 10.0.1.0/24 public-2 Public AZ 2 Load Balancer, NAT Gateway 10.0.2.0/24 private-app-1 Private AZ 1 EC2 instance running WordPress 10.0.3.0/24 private-app-2 Private AZ 2 EC2 instance running WordPress 10.0.4.0/24 private-db-1 Private AZ 1 RDS database 10.0.5.0/24 private-db-2 Private AZ 2 RDS database 10.0.6.0/24 Steps
  7. Create the VPC. In the VPC console, create a VPC with a CIDR block such as 10.0.0.0/16 and give it a clear name tag.
  8. Create the six subnets. Create each subnet from the table above, choosing the right Availability Zone for each one.
  9. Create and attach an Internet Gateway. The Internet Gateway (IGW) is the door between the VPC and the internet. Attach it to your VPC.
  10. Create a public route table. Add a route sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet Gateway, then associate this route table with the two public subnets. A subnet is only "public" because its route table points to the Internet Gateway. The private subnets have no such route, which is why nothing on the internet can reach them directly. The private subnets still need to download packages and updates, which is what the NAT Gateways in the next part are for. Part 3: Networking Setup, NAT Gateways and Security Groups Private servers cannot be reached from the internet, but they still need to go out to it for software updates and WordPress packages. A NAT Gateway allows outbound connections from private subnets while blocking inbound ones. Security groups then act as firewalls around each layer. Create the NAT Gateways
  11. Allocate two Elastic IP addresses, one for each NAT Gateway.
  12. Create a NAT Gateway in each public subnet, so there is one per Availability Zone. If one zone fails, the other zone's servers keep their outbound access.
  13. Create two private route tables, one per Availability Zone. In each, add a route sending 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT Gateway in the same zone.
  14. Associate each private route table with the private subnets in its zone. Create the security groups The rule of thumb is least privilege: each layer accepts traffic only from the layer directly in front of it. Security group Attached to Allows inbound from Port alb-sg Application Load Balancer Anywhere on the internet 80 (HTTP), plus 443 if you add HTTPS web-sg EC2 WordPress instances alb-sg only 80 db-sg RDS MySQL database web-sg only 3306 efs-sg EFS file system web-sg only 2049 (NFS) Because each group references the previous one instead of an IP range, a visitor can only reach WordPress through the Load Balancer, and only the WordPress servers can reach the database. Part 4: Database Setup, MySQL Database and EFS WordPress stores two kinds of data, and each gets its own managed service. Amazon RDS holds the content (posts, users, settings), and Amazon EFS holds the files (themes, plugins, uploads). With two web servers, shared storage matters: an image uploaded through one server must also appear on the other. Create the MySQL database on RDS
  15. Create a DB subnet group that contains the two private database subnets, one in each Availability Zone.
  16. Create the database. Choose the MySQL engine and a small instance class to keep costs low. Set the database name, the admin username and a strong password, and write them down, because WordPress needs them later.
  17. Place it in the VPC. Select your VPC and the DB subnet group, and turn off public access.
  18. Attach the db-sg security group so that only the WordPress servers can connect on port 3306.
  19. Copy the database endpoint once the instance is available. You will enter it into the WordPress configuration. Create the EFS file system
  20. Create an EFS file system in the same VPC.
  21. Create a mount target in each private application subnet, using the efs-sg security group.
  22. Note the file system ID. Both EC2 instances will mount it to share the WordPress files.

Part 5: Compute Setup, EC2 Instances and Application Load Balancer
This part brings the site to life. Two EC2 instances run WordPress in private subnets, and an Application Load Balancer in the public subnets is the only door visitors use.
Launch and configure the EC2 instances

  1. Launch two EC2 instances, one in each private application subnet. Attach the web-sg security group and do not assign a public IP address.
  2. Attach an IAM role to the instances so they can work securely with other AWS services.
  3. Install the web stack. Install a web server (Apache or Nginx), PHP and the MySQL client. The NAT Gateways make these downloads possible.
  4. Mount the EFS file system on the WordPress directory so both servers share the same files.
  5. Install WordPress and point its configuration file at the RDS endpoint, database name, username and password from Part 4. Create the Application Load Balancer
  6. Create a target group for HTTP on port 80 and register both EC2 instances. The health check lets the Load Balancer stop sending traffic to an unhealthy server. WordPress often redirects the home page, so accept redirect codes in the health check if it reports unhealthy.
  7. Create an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in the two public subnets with the alb-sg security group.
  8. Add a listener on port 80 that forwards traffic to the target group.
  9. Open the ALB DNS name in your browser. When both targets show as healthy, the WordPress setup page appears. Complete the WordPress installation through the ALB DNS name rather than an instance address, so the site URL WordPress saves is the one visitors will actually use. How a visitor request travels
  10. The visitor's browser sends a request to the ALB DNS name.
  11. The Load Balancer picks a healthy EC2 instance and forwards the request.
  12. WordPress on that instance reads the content from RDS and the files from EFS.
  13. The page returns to the visitor through the Load Balancer. Part 6: Conclusion and Clean-up The result is a production-style WordPress site: visitors reach it through the Load Balancer, the servers and database stay private, and two Availability Zones keep it running if one fails. What I learned • Networking is the hardest and most important part. Most problems come from route tables or security groups, so check those first when something does not connect. • Private subnets are a big security win. Nothing sensitive is reachable from the internet. • Shared storage matters. Without EFS, two WordPress servers would show different files. • High availability means duplication. Two zones, two NAT Gateways and two servers remove single points of failure. Clean up to avoid charges NAT Gateways, the RDS database and the Load Balancer are billed by the hour, even when idle. Delete resources in this order, because AWS blocks deleting something that another resource still depends on:
  14. Delete the Application Load Balancer, then its target group.
  15. Terminate both EC2 instances.
  16. Delete the RDS database.
  17. Delete the EFS mount targets, then the EFS file system.
  18. Delete both NAT Gateways, then release the Elastic IP addresses.
  19. Delete the custom security groups and route tables.
  20. Detach and delete the Internet Gateway.
  21. Delete the subnets, then the VPC. Finally, open the Billing console the next day and confirm no unexpected charges are appearing. Final thoughts Building a 3-tier architecture turned AWS from a long list of services into one system I understand. If you are learning cloud or DevOps, it is one of the best hands-on projects to start with.

At that stage, I could route a request to the frontend or backend. But there was another problem I didn't want to ignore. My onprem was considered alive.

Every time someone changes the application, who should be responsible for deploying that change to Kubernetes?

I could keep building an image locally, pushing it to a registry, and manually updating a Deployment. That works for the first few tests, it did wonderfully. However, it isn't the workflow I wanted for a platform that would host more applications.

1. The problem wasn't building a Docker image

I already had application containers and a Kubernetes cluster that could run them. The application also had ClusterIP Services and an HTTPRoute, so the traffic side had a place to go.

The problem was the release process.

I didn't want the normal deployment path to look like this:

Developer changes code
        |
        v
Build an image manually
        |
        v
Push image to registry
        |
        v
SSH to a server / access cluster
        |
        v
kubectl set image or kubectl apply
        |
        v
Hope the live state matches what is in Git

It has a lot of problem to be honest, like manually building image? okay

It has a lot of problem to be honest, like manually building image? okay, but the last step is the real problem. Once a person changes a live Deployment manually, the cluster might be ahead of, or simply different from, the version recorded in the repository.

That also makes rollback confusing. Am I reverting a Git commit? Reusing an older image? Or undoing someone's manual change? too much headache.

I wanted a simpler answer:

Application repositories produce artifacts. The GitOps repository declares desired versions. Argo CD owns reconciliation.

That is not a magical security boundary, by the way. A pipeline with permission to modify the GitOps repository can still influence what the cluster will deploy. But at least it doesn't need a direct Kubernetes API credential to perform the normal delivery path.

2. Three repositories, two kinds of responsibility

My application was split into a frontend and a backend. Each had its own source code, Dockerfile, and CI workflow. A separate cluster-management repository held the Kubernetes manifests.

The intended flow was:

FRONTEND SOURCE REPO                  BACKEND SOURCE REPO
       |                                     |
    push main                             push main
       |                                     |
       v                                     v
  GitHub Actions                        GitHub Actions
  test / build                          test / build
       |                                     |
       v                                     v
  GHCR frontend                         GHCR backend
  image: sha-FE                         image: sha-BE
       |                                     |
       v                                     v
 frontend-image.yaml                   backend-image.yaml
       \                                     /
        \                                   /
         +----- cluster-management --------+
                         |
                         v
                      Argo CD
                         |
                         v
                Kubernetes staging
               frontend + backend

There are two separate concerns here.

Component What it owns What it should not own in this design
Frontend GitHub Actions Frontend checks, image build, GHCR publish, frontend image reference update Direct Kubernetes deployment
Backend GitHub Actions Backend checks, image build, GHCR publish, backend image reference update Frontend image reference or direct Kubernetes deployment
GHCR The published container images Which release is currently desired in staging
cluster-management Git repository Kubernetes configuration and desired image references Building application images
Argo CD Reading desired state, rendering manifests, and reconciling Kubernetes Building source code or deciding an image tag on its own

Notice that the frontend release and backend release have different commit IDs.

That seems obvious when you look at the two source repositories. But it matters when you design the automation. There is no reason to pretend that both services share one source commit.

3. Why I didn't give GitHub Actions a kubeconfig

I considered the direct model first: build an image in CI, then run kubectl set image from the GitHub Actions runner.

It would have been relatively straightforward. But it also meant giving the CI workflow Kubernetes credentials and making the runner part of the cluster deployment control path.

I didn't want that as the default for this project.

Instead, the access model in my runbook separated three relationships:

GitHub Actions  ---> GHCR
    publishes the application image

GitHub Actions  ---> GitOps Git repository
    writes only the application's desired image reference

Argo CD         ---> GitOps Git repository
    reads the desired state

Argo CD         ---> Kubernetes API
    reconciles the workload

So no kubeconfig, Kubernetes ServiceAccount token, or Argo API token needed to be copied into the application CI workflow for the normal deployment process.

However, I want to be precise about what that does, and doesn't, improve.

Removing direct cluster credentials from CI reduces one class of exposure. It doesn't make a compromised CI runner harmless.

If a workflow has permission to modify the GitOps repository, an attacker who compromises that workflow could potentially change the desired state that Argo CD eventually applies. So the GitOps write credential is still a form of deployment authority, even if it doesn't directly access the Kubernetes API.

But there is another side to this.

Because my GitOps repository is private, Argo CD also needs GitHub credentials to read it. Ideally, those credentials should only have read access.

And since Argo CD is running inside my on-premises Kubernetes cluster, I also have to consider what happens if that environment gets compromised.

An attacker who gains access to Argo CD's repository credentials could potentially use them according to the permissions assigned to those credentials. If those permissions are broader than read-only, the impact could be greater. A compromise of Argo CD itself could also expose its Kubernetes access, which is a separate concern.

So technically, I'm not eliminating credential-related risks. I'm separating responsibilities and trying to limit what each component is allowed to do.

In my case, some repository access relied on temporary, account-linked SSH credentials because of restrictions on using deploy keys. That was an acceptable workaround for getting this non-production lab running, but I wouldn't consider it an ideal long-term permission model.

After all, a credential tied to a personal GitHub account could inherit permissions beyond what the workflow or Argo CD actually needs.
For a more mature implementation, I would prefer a dedicated GitHub App or similarly constrained identity, protected branches or approval gates as appropriate, and short-lived credentials where available. I would also limit Argo CD's destinations and resource permissions through an AppProject. None of these safeguards should be assumed to exist just because GitOps is installed.

That distinction is important to me. I don't want to call something "least privilege" merely because the YAML looks neat.

4. The real design problem: two CI pipelines editing the same file

Originally, I could describe frontend and backend images together inside the staging kustomization.yaml:

images:
  - name: ghcr.io/example/frontend
    newTag: sha-FRONTEND
  - name: ghcr.io/example/backend
    newTag: sha-BACKEND

That is a perfectly valid Kustomize pattern.

But if the frontend and backend pipelines both update the same file, a small timing problem appears:

12:00  Frontend CI checks out GitOps commit A
12:01  Backend CI checks out GitOps commit A
12:03  Frontend CI updates the shared YAML, pushes commit B
12:04  Backend CI tries to push its edit based on A
12:04  Push rejected: the remote branch changed

This doesn't automatically mean data loss. Git rejected the non-fast-forward push. But now the pipeline needs to reconcile its change with the remote branch.

I didn't want both pipelines repeatedly rewriting the same shared image list. So I split the ownership into two small patch files.

cluster-management/
  apps/
    marketplace/
      base/
        frontend/
          deployment.yaml
          service.yaml
        backend/
          deployment.yaml
          service.yaml
      overlays/
        staging/
          kustomization.yaml
          patches/
            frontend-image.yaml    <- frontend CI owns this
            backend-image.yaml     <- backend CI owns this
          routing/
            httproute.yaml

The base contains the reusable workload definitions. The overlay contains staging-specific configuration, including the selected images.

In the staging kustomization.yaml, the relevant part is:

apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

namespace: demo-staging

resources:
  - ../../base

patches:
  - path: patches/frontend-image.yaml
  - path: patches/backend-image.yaml

These are simplified examples. A real overlay may also include ConfigMaps, NetworkPolicies, routes, and other resources, which need to be declared in the appropriate base or overlay.

The frontend's patch can be as small as:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: frontend
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: frontend
          image: ghcr.io/example/frontend:sha-FRONTEND_COMMIT

The backend has a separate file with its own Deployment, container name, and image.

One technical detail here: a strategic-merge patch identifies the container entry by its name. That name must match the actual container name in the base Deployment. I would validate the rendered manifest rather than assume the patch changed the right thing.

Splitting the files does not make concurrent Git pushes automatically safe. It just means that when one runner rebases on top of the other's commit, the edits are usually independent and easier to merge.

5. The image tag is a release record, not latest

I wanted the deployed image reference to point to a specific source revision.

Each source workflow publishes an image tagged with its own commit SHA:

ghcr.io/example/frontend:sha-
ghcr.io/example/backend:sha-

So staging might contain this combination:

Frontend = sha-a1b2c3...
Backend  = sha-d4e5f6...

The backend does not need to restart just because the frontend changed. Their Deployment Pod templates change independently.

A commit-based tag is also easier to trace than latest. However, a tag is still a mutable registry reference unless the registry prevents overwrites. For stronger artifact immutability, image digests such as @sha256:... are preferable. The source design used SHA-based tags; it should not be described as having guaranteed digest-pinned deployments.

There is another limitation: the frontend in this project was built with Vite, so environment values such as the API base URL may be embedded during npm run build. Those VITE_* build arguments are not a substitute for Kubernetes runtime Secrets. I have to validate the target environment when building an artifact for staging.

6. What the pipeline actually needs to do

I don't think the most useful article is one that pastes 300 lines of GitHub Actions YAML without explaining anything.

The important sequence is:

  1. Run the source repository's checks.
  2. Build and publish the appropriate image to GHCR.
  3. Check out the GitOps repository with Git write permission.
  4. Update only the component's image patch.
  5. Render Kustomize and confirm the intended image appears.
  6. Commit and push that desired-state change, handling a concurrent push safely.
  7. Let Argo CD detect and reconcile the new Git revision.

For the GHCR part, the workflow needs only the permissions appropriate for publishing the package. A representative excerpt is:

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

# In a build job after source checkout and tests:
# - authenticate to ghcr.io with the workflow GITHUB_TOKEN
# - build for the intended node architecture
# - push ghcr.io/example/frontend:sha-${{ github.sha }}

That is a workflow sketch, not a complete GitHub Actions file. GitHub's official container-publishing documentation describes GITHUB_TOKEN with packages: write for this use case.

I deliberately kept the GitOps write key separate from the GHCR authentication. The built-in GITHUB_TOKEN is normally scoped to the repository running the workflow; it is not automatically authorized to write to an unrelated private GitOps repository.

Validate the change before committing it

Before pushing a new image reference, I would render the overlay:

cd cluster-management

kubectl kustomize apps/marketplace/overlays/staging \
  > /tmp/staging-rendered.yaml

test -s /tmp/staging-rendered.yaml

grep -n 'image:' /tmp/staging-rendered.yaml

I would then confirm that both rendered Deployments contain the intended image references. That also catches mistakes in patch names, paths, and Kustomize structure before Argo CD sees the commit.

This test is static validation. It does not prove that Kubernetes pulled the image, started a Pod, or served a request.

What about simultaneous GitOps updates?

GitHub Actions' concurrency setting can serialize jobs or runs within one repository. But my frontend and backend workflows were in different repositories, so a concurrency group in the frontend repository does not coordinate with the backend repository's group.

A simplified push strategy is:

# Run from the GitOps checkout after committing a component patch.
# This assumes a clean commit that can be safely rebased.

for attempt in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  git fetch origin main
  git rebase origin/main || {
    echo 'Rebase conflict: stop and investigate.' >&2
    exit 1
  }

  if git push origin HEAD:main; then
    echo 'GitOps update pushed.'
    break
  fi

  if [ "$attempt" -eq 5 ]; then
    echo 'GitOps push still failing after retries.' >&2
    exit 1
  fi

done

Why not just force-push? Because force-pushing from a CI pipeline risks overwriting the other component's deployment update. In the normal case, separate patch files let Git rebase independent commits cleanly. A genuine rebase conflict should stop the pipeline rather than be hidden.

This is still only one approach. A pull request into a protected GitOps branch would offer stronger review and audit gates, at the cost of another approval step. For staging, the source runbook intentionally favored direct automation.

7. Argo CD owns the cluster-facing part

For this project, Argo CD itself was managed with Helm. That was a platform installation decision. The application's desired state was managed with Kustomize and watched by an Argo CD Application.

The relationship was:

Helm: install/manage Argo CD itself
                  |
                  v
Argo CD Application: watch the GitOps source
                  |
                  v
Kustomize: render staging resources
                  |
                  v
Kubernetes: reconcile Deployments and Services

Argo CD natively supports Kustomize sources. The application points at the desired repository path; I didn't need a separate kubectl apply -k command in the application pipeline.

A reduced Application example would look like this:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: demo-staging
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: staging
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/example/cluster-management.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/marketplace/overlays/staging
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: demo-staging
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      enabled: true
      selfHeal: true
      prune: false

That example assumes the AppProject, repository credentials, namespace, and required RBAC already exist. A private repository also needs appropriate credentials. The repoURL shown here is illustrative, not a live repository.

There are two Argo CD settings I didn't want to treat casually:

  • selfHeal allows Argo CD to reconcile certain live-cluster drift back toward Git's desired state.
  • prune allows deletion of resources that are no longer present in the desired state when automated pruning is enabled.

I preferred starting with manual sync and no automatic pruning, inspecting the diff, then introducing automated sync and self-healing only after the repository accurately represented the existing application. Pruning was a later, separate decision.

That order matters. Automatically reconciling an incomplete or incorrect Git repository can break an application very efficiently.

One more point: Synced is about the relationship between the desired and live resource state. Healthy is a separate assessment. Neither one alone proves that the application's user-facing endpoint works correctly.

8. What I would verify end to end

My runbooks contain detailed acceptance procedures, including a frontend test before activating the backend workflow. They don't contain complete captured logs for every step, so I will describe the validation procedure and expected outcome, not invent a passed test transcript.

Check Command or location What it proves if successful
Source validation GitHub Actions job logs The relevant checks completed
Image published GHCR package and tag An image reference exists in the registry
Desired state updated GitOps repository commit and patch diff CI wrote the intended source SHA into Git
Manifests render kubectl kustomize The selected overlay produces valid YAML and intended image references
Argo has accepted source kubectl get application -n argocd Argo CD sees the desired revision and reports sync/health status
Pod template updated kubectl get deployment -o jsonpath=... The workload spec contains the new image reference
Rollout completes kubectl rollout status The Deployment rollout reached Kubernetes' completion criteria
App responds App-specific HTTP health/smoke tests The tested endpoint responded through the selected route

For example, in an example namespace:

kubectl get application demo-staging -n argocd

kubectl get deployment frontend -n demo-staging \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}'

kubectl rollout status deployment/frontend \
  -n demo-staging --timeout=180s

Then I would repeat the test with the backend, checking that a backend-only change does not modify the frontend's desired image reference.

There is also a useful negative test: deliberately modify a managed Deployment in the cluster only in a disposable test environment, and check whether self-healing restores the value declared in Git. That's a controlled test of reconciliation, not a suggested operating habit.

The important distinction is that a successful build doesn't mean a successful release. Publishing an image is not the same as writing desired state, and writing desired state is not the same as confirming a healthy application.

9. Two problems that belong in the GitOps story

So while creating it, i have noted some issues that appeared when Argo CD took ownership of existing resources and private repositories.

The first was an application that repeatedly appeared OutOfSync. When developing this, I had included a system-managed metadata.generation value in a Deployment manifest. That value is maintained by Kubernetes rather than being application desired configuration. My note records removing it from the declarative manifest. I would check the live diff and refresh result before treating that as a universally proven root cause for any OutOfSync condition.

The second was a private repository access problem. So I recorded an SSH-agent-related error while Argo CD tried to resolve a Git revision. A repository Secret had also been scoped to a particular Argo CD project, while other Applications needed the same repository. That was a reasonable permission-scope hypothesis to investigate, not enough evidence by itself to say that every SSH_AUTH_SOCK error is caused by project scoping.

These two examples gave me a practical reminder: GitOps introduces its own layer of configuration and debugging. The source revision, rendered manifest, repository credential, AppProject, and live Kubernetes object all need to be inspected separately.

10. The trade-offs I would keep visible

This architecture improved clarity, but I wouldn't call it perfect.

Direct-to-main staging: The workflow I created deploys staging candidates from main. There was no pre-merge review gate in that model. A failing CI job stops that image from becoming the next desired version, but it doesn't remove the bad commit from the source branch.

Temporary Git credentials: I used a dedicated SSH key associated with a personal GitHub account. That should be treated as technical debt, with access narrowed and credentials rotated when an organization-approved service identity is available.

Two independent source repositories: A separate image patch per component reduced file contention, but the pipelines still shared one GitOps branch. A push/rebase retry or an approved merge workflow was needed to handle concurrency.

Tags versus digests: SHA-based tags improved traceability. They did not by themselves prove registry immutability.

Database migrations: I intentionally kept automatic database migration out of the first application-image workflow. Database schema changes need their own compatibility, execution, and recovery strategy. A separate migration Job can be introduced later once that contract is clear.

Rollbacks: Reverting a GitOps image change can trigger Argo CD to redeploy an earlier application image. That does not automatically undo a database migration or guarantee compatibility with external dependencies.

11. What I learned

For me, the interesting part wasn't that GitHub Actions could run a Docker build. That's the easy part, and of course that the world of devops is huge.

The more useful decision was defining who was allowed to change what.

GitHub Actions could produce a frontend or backend image and propose the intended version through Git. Argo CD was responsible for translating that version into a Kubernetes deployment. And the two source repositories needed separate release records so one team's change wouldn't accidentally replace another component's desired version.

I would still tighten the credentials and add stronger release gates before applying this model to more sensitive environments. But for this non-production platform, separating build, desired state, and reconciliation gave me a structure I could reason about.

The next article will move from who is allowed to deploy to which network connections workloads are allowed to receive: testing Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rather than assuming namespace separation provides isolation.

References

  • Argo CD: Automated Sync Policy
  • Argo CD: Kustomize
  • GitHub: Publishing Docker Images
  • GitHub: Control Workflow Concurrency
  • GitHub Actions: Secure Use Reference
